claims.text: The claim that both goods and services consumer spending rose in Q1 2024 is contradicted by the BEA second estimate: services increased while goods decreased.

citations.quotation:
The increase in consumer spending reflected an increase in services that was partly offset by a
decrease in goods. Within services, the leading contributors to the increase were health care as well
as financial services and insurance. Within goods, the leading contributors to the decrease were
motor vehicles and parts as well as gasoline and other energy goods.

counterarguments.text: Overall consumer spending did increase in Q1 2024 and was a primary driver of GDP growth, but this was driven by services only, not goods.

citations.quotation:
The increase in the first quarter primarily reflected increases in consumer spending and housing
investment that were partly offset by a decrease in inventory investment.

limitations: No passage in the sources states that goods spending rose in Q1 2024; no contrary evidence supporting the claim was found, so the gap remains a gap and is not itself proof.

The GDP figure alone establishes only the aggregate growth rate; it cannot establish the composition of spending by goods versus services, the causes of the changes, income distribution effects, or real-time levels of wellbeing.
Excerpts are partial; some table values (e.g., specific contribution magnitudes) are not fully legible in the supplied text.
Publication date (2024-05-30) is declared, not independently verified.

citation.quotation:
Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 1.3 percent in the first quarter of
2024, according to the “second” estimate.
In the fourth quarter of 2023, real GDP increased 3.4 percent.

The GDP estimate for the first quarter was revised down 0.3 percentage point from the “advance”
estimate, primarily reflecting a downward revision to consumer spending.
